new_entities.name: Adaptive servo-ventilation for central sleep apnea in HFrEF
aliases: ASV for CSA with reduced-EF heart failure
adaptive servo-ventilation in central sleep apnea and systolic heart failure
new_entities.description: Use of adaptive servo-ventilation to treat predominant central sleep apnea or Cheyne-Stokes respiration in adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

edges.effect_quant: In SERVE-HF, adaptive servo-ventilation increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.28) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.34) in symptomatic HFrEF with predominant central sleep apnea. Subsequent SERVE-HF analyses continued to show excess cardiovascular death rather than reassurance, even though smaller pre-SERVE studies had shown improvement in apnea metrics.
edges.population: adults with symptomatic chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and predominant central sleep apnea or Cheyne-Stokes respiration
edges.mechanism: Although ASV suppresses central events and improves nocturnal ventilation, in HFrEF it may adversely affect vulnerable hemodynamics or arrhythmic risk in ways that outweigh surrogate sleep benefits.
edges.summary: This is one of the clearest harmful edges in the sleep block. In CSA plus HFrEF, ASV improves respiratory physiology but the major randomized hard-outcome trial showed excess mortality, so it should not be framed as a benign sleep-only intervention in this phenotype.
edges.caveats: The harm signal is phenotype specific: it applies to reduced-EF heart failure with predominant central sleep apnea, not to all causes of CSA. Smaller earlier studies and non-HFrEF cohorts can look more favorable because they were focused on surrogate endpoints rather than mortality.

evidence.citation: CowieMR et al 2015 N Engl J Med
evidence.notes: Adaptive Servo-Ventilation for Central Sleep Apnea in Systolic Heart Failure. SERVE-HF.

effect_quant.comparator: all-cause mortality with adaptive servo-ventilation plus guideline-based care versus control in SERVE-HF
